comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: The English and Dutch tracks appear in this order in Article 10.2. The English route is selected on official order. Appendix III and the current course guide establish 60 EC per year, with two separately restricted 6 EC choices in year two and 30 EC of elective space in year three. Article 9.1 sets prior participation in Discovering Anthropology for Global History of Inequality and Ethnographic Research Methodology 1, 90 EC from years one and two for the bachelor project, and project registration for Anthropology for Society. The official project page confirms independent fieldwork and an individual thesis. The programme page identifies three profiles with academic, policy or creative outputs, within the credited curriculum. Separate practical attendance, language diagnostic and first-year study advice rules do not add credits. The Anthropology for Society course specifies completion of project fieldwork before taking it and locates the public-facing profile output in that 6 EC course.

alternatives.label: Culture, inequality and visual social inquiry
alternatives.concept: Studies how people experience inequality and social change through sociology, global and Indigenous histories, and visual media. Students practise qualitative inquiry, interpret cultural objects and representations, and make a short documentary.
alternatives.labelReason: The schedule integrates interpretive social inquiry with power, development, historical and audiovisual representation.
progression: First-year PPD, sociology, history and introductory media precede advanced work in civil society, media and historical interpretation. The legal gateway precedes public international law.

alternatives.label: Development, governance and social justice
alternatives.concept: Studies how political institutions, laws and economic policies shape inequality and social change. Students combine qualitative inquiry with political theory, public economics and the study of rights, including refugee protection and EU citizenship.
alternatives.labelReason: A two-course economics sequence, political philosophy and constitutional and EU law build a focus on institutions, redistribution and public authority.
alternatives.distinctness: Five courses differ in each direction (37.5 EC). Economics, political philosophy, public economics, comparative constitutional law and EU law take the place of introductory film, gender histories, African art and heritage, environmental media, and documentary.
progression: First-year sociology, economics, methods and the legal gateway precede public economics and advanced legal study. Qualitative inquiry supports later work on civil society.

selection.assessment: The closest option connects qualitative inquiry with histories of power and interpretation of cultural forms. A distinct policy direction adds economics and legal institutions. Separate criminology and religion directions would weaken the anthropological basis and cannot sustain a distinct comparable curriculum. Communication, visual and media study are covered within the closest option.

blocks: Both examine the historical formation of global inequalities. UCR focuses on empires and their contested legacies.
Both trace the development of social thought. UCR focuses on sociology, modernity and its relationship to empire.
VU introduces anthropology as a discipline. UCR develops related social and cultural inquiry across sociology, history and media.
UCR studies empire and decolonial social thought. VU applies anthropological methods and theories directly to development.
UCR draws on political science, economics and law. VU approaches political and economic life through anthropology.
VU studies religion in digital settings as a dedicated subject.
VU continues applied anthropology and profile development in its third masterclass.
VU develops the chosen profile further in its fourth masterclass.
UCR examines gendered histories and inequality. The VU choice focuses specifically on gender inequalities.
UCR studies environmental justice and how media represent environmental change. This VU choice centres the human dimension of sustainable development.
Both use questions of justice to study social change. UCR focuses on environmental justice and collective action.
UCR studies migration within law, history and sociology. VU examines migration and belonging as a dedicated subject.
Urban life appears in related UCR social inquiry. VU gives urban studies a dedicated course.
UCR covers ethics and qualitative research assumptions. VU separately examines how scientific knowledge is produced and justified.
VU connects anthropological findings with a profile and wider audience. UCR practises public communication in several courses.
Both develop academic argument and responsible source use. UCR also includes personal development and community engagement.
Both practise qualitative inquiry, including observation and interviews. VU develops these methods in a dedicated ethnographic sequence.
VU gives research methodology its own foundation course. UCR develops design and measurement in Research Methods & Statistics and interpretive inquiry in Qualitative Research Methodology.
VU introduces the anthropology profiles through dedicated masterclasses.
VU continues profile exploration in a second first-year masterclass.
VU reserves 30 EC for a minor, internship, study abroad or electives.
VU prepares students for their own fieldwork through advanced ethnographic design and practice. UCR develops related qualitative methods in course projects.
VU requires an individual ethnographic thesis based on independent fieldwork. UCR’s optional independent research sits outside the displayed schedules.
Both teach descriptive and inferential statistics. UCR also studies general research design and measurement.

notes.text: VU teaches ethnographic methods across several years and requires an 18 EC project with independent fieldwork and an individual thesis. UCR offers related qualitative research, cultural analysis and policy study. Its optional independent research is separate from the 180 EC schedules shown.

audience.programmeDescription: At VU Amsterdam, Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology studies how global changes affect everyday life. Students examine identity, power and inequality and learn ethnographic methods through observation, interviews and fieldwork.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers two ways to explore related questions. One combines qualitative social inquiry with history and visual culture. The other studies how public institutions, economic policy and law shape social change.

curriculum.limitation: The second year shows one example from each of two required choice groups. In the third year, 30 EC are available for elective study. Students need 90 EC from the first two years to begin the bachelor project and complete its fieldwork before taking Anthropology for Society.
